concept_name: Ionisation Enthalpy: The Energy Cost of Removing an Electron
source_book: NCERT Chemistry Class 11, Ch.3 'Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties', §3.7.1(c) — ionisation enthalpy: the definition (ΔᵢH₁), the size/pull link, periodic and group trends, successive ionisation enthalpies and the shell-structure evidence they carry, and the Be/B and N/O anomalies where the screening model measurably fails — chapter-index scope and vocabulary reference only (the terms 'ionisation enthalpy', 'successive ionisation enthalpies', ΔᵢH₁ meet the student's own textbook and exam); teaching, sequence and phrasing authored from first principles. NCERT Exemplar consulted for misconception beliefs only (every electron costs about the same; ionisation energy just rises across a period); no problem text, figure or worked example imported. Every ionisation enthalpy shown is a direct citation (CRC 97th / NIST ASD, OS_IE), never computed by the engine; every radius, Z_eff and Slater screening figure is independently re-derived from the exact hydrogenic radial functions and Slater's rules. Second concept of the Ch.3 periodicity wave (desk feat/chemistry-periodicity), second concept on the field_3d orbital_shapes surface.

real_world_anchor.primary: Sodium must be stored under oil; neon needs no protection at all. How easily an atom gives up its outer electron decides how it behaves, and that ease is a measured number: 495.8 kJ/mol for sodium, 2080.7 for neon.

n.name: principal quantum number of the drawn valence shell

k.name: electron index — the k-th electron removed (IE index = charge + 1)

ie_measured_hud.formula: IE_k for the species/index on screen, printed 'IEk = <value> kJ/mol (measured)' with a real <sub> k index; em dash for an anion or an index past the citation

staircase_rung_count.formula: osIeDrawCount(element) = valence electron count (neutral) + 2 -- e.g. Na 3, Mg 4, Al 5 -- derived so the cliff always lands one rung from the right edge, keyed to the NEUTRAL atom so the axis never rescales under a charge drag

radius_hud_pm.formula: r90_pm, printed 'r = <n> pm (90%)', or with the ', spherical average' suffix on an open p subshell (from S2/F on — never on Li, Be, or a full subshell like Ne)

z_eff_hud.formula: Z_eff, printed '(Slater)' -- S7 only in this concept (38b: the symbol is the prerequisite's, not taught in this concept's own core states)

delta_ratio_display.formula: IE_2 / IE_1, arithmetic on two citations, printed '9.2 x' on S5's formula surface

constraints: electron count is exactly conserved in every ionisation equation (Na 11e- -> Na+ 10e- + 1e-; Na+ 10e- -> Na2+ 9e- + 1e-)
charge balances on both sides of every ionisation equation (0 = +1 + -1; +1 = +2 + -1)
every ionisation enthalpy on any surface is a citation from OS_IE (CRC 97th / NIST ASD), stamped (measured); the engine never computes an IE
the model series (Slater-hydrogenic 13.6 Z_eff^2/n^2) is drawn only beside the measurement, in its own colour/dash/mark, and is never stamped (measured)
the staircase rung count is keyed to the neutral atom's valence electron count, never to the live charge, so the axis never rescales under a marker mid-state
ion charge is always an integer in {-3 ... +3}; no fractional charge is ever shown

scene_composition.text: sodium's outer electron, before removal
removing it costs energy — measured
495.8 kilojoules per mole for sodium

tts_sentences.text_en: Sodium must be stored under oil; neon needs no protection at all.
Pulling one electron off an atom costs energy — the ionisation enthalpy, ΔᵢH₁, also written IE₁.
Sodium's cost: 495.8 kilojoules per mole, measured.

scene_composition.text: lithium and fluorine, same outer shell
fluorine has far more protons pulling
520.2 versus 1681.0 kilojoules per mole

tts_sentences.text_en: Lithium and fluorine both keep their outermost electron in the second shell, but fluorine feels far more protons with little screening.
Lithium's electron costs 520.2 kilojoules per mole; fluorine's costs 1681.0.
Fluorine's outer subshell is only part filled, so radius reads as a spherical average.

scene_composition.text: across period two, element by element
size falls while removal cost rises
371 down to 72 picometres; 520 up to 2081

tts_sentences.text_en: Across period two, rising nuclear charge pulls each shell in — lithium 371 picometres down to neon 72 — while the same charge raises the removal cost, step by step: 520 up to 2081 kilojoules per mole.

scene_composition.text: down a group, one more shell each step
outer electron sits farther from the nucleus
520.2, then 495.8, then 418.8 kilojoules per mole

tts_sentences.text_en: Down a group, sodium's outer electron starts in a new, farther shell than lithium's — potassium's farther still, shell four.
Farther out and screened by more inner electrons, removal costs less each step: 520.2, then 495.8, then 418.8 kilojoules per mole.

scene_composition.text: sodium's staircase, three rungs, fixed
the second electron costs nine times more
495.8, then 4562, then 6910.3 kilojoules per mole

misconception_watch.belief: Every electron costs about the same to remove.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: The second electron's rung stands about nine times taller than the first electron's rung on one staircase, and the HUD reading steps from 495.8 up to 4562.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: The second electron comes from a full inner shell, much closer to the nucleus — that is the jump.

tts_sentences.text_en: Sodium's staircase is fixed on screen: three rungs, complete before anything moves.
The first electron costs 495.8 kilojoules per mole.
The second climbs the same staircase to 4562 — the jump, nine times taller.
The second electron comes from a full inner shell, closer to the nucleus, causing the jump.
The third rung: 6910.3.

scene_composition.text: the staircase swaps with each element
where the jump falls counts the valence electrons
sodium one, magnesium two, aluminium three

tts_sentences.text_en: Now the whole staircase swaps with the element, and the jump moves.
Sodium's one valence electron puts the jump after the first rung.
Magnesium has two electrons: 737.7, 1450.7, then the jump at 7732.7, after the second rung.
Aluminium has three: 577.5, 1816.7, 2744.8, then 11577.
The jump position counts the valence electrons.

scene_composition.text: measured cost against the screening model
the measured trace dips; the model does not

misconception_watch.belief: Across a period the ionisation cost only rises.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: The amber measured trace dips at boron and at oxygen while the cyan model trace rises through both points.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: The rise holds shell by shell — a new subshell at boron and a shared orbital at oxygen each make removal cheaper.

tts_sentences.text_en: Measured, the cost dips at boron: 899.5 down to 800.6 kilojoules per mole.
Boron's new electron sits in a different, higher subshell — the model, rising smoothly, misses this.
Measured, oxygen dips: 1402.3 down to 1313.9; two electrons now share one orbital, a cause not shown here.
The axis is compressed so both traces fit.

scene_composition.text: choose any element
choose any charge
size and removal cost respond together

tts_sentences.text_en: Now choose any element and any charge, and watch the size and the removal cost respond together.

aha_moment.statement: Sodium's second electron costs nine times the first — a shell edge, not a slope.
aha_moment.visual_confirmation: the staircase's second rung stands about nine times taller than the first, and the HUD reading steps from 495.8 to 4562 kJ/mol as the marker climbs

regeneration_variants.label: Same energy-cost idea, argon's first ionisation instead of sodium's
regeneration_variants.physical_world: Argon, a noble gas with a full outer shell, still gives up its outermost electron for a real, measured energy cost — far higher than sodium's, because argon's outer electrons are held by a much larger effective nuclear charge with no easy shell to empty into.
regeneration_variants.same_physics: Identical reasoning: the ionisation enthalpy is a citation from the same measured table, the removal is the same all-or-nothing cut, and the same successive-IE staircase logic applies — only the element and its numbers change, never the physics.
